anatomy.lede: Seen from above, a horseshoe crab is a domed shield, a hinged rear plate and a spike of a tail. Almost everything else — legs, gills, mouth — is tucked away underneath.

hotspots.label: Compound eye
hotspots.text: Two large compound eyes sit on the sides of the shell. Their main job is finding mates during the spawning season.

hotspots.label: Head shield
hotspots.text: The front, horseshoe-shaped shield covers the head and the six pairs of appendages used for feeding and walking.

hotspots.label: Hinge
hotspots.text: A hinge joins the head shield to the spiny rear section, which shelters the book gills underneath.

hotspots.label: Tail (telson)
hotspots.text: The long tail is harmless. It works as a rudder in the water and as a lever to flip the animal upright when a wave turns it over.

senses.lede: The horseshoe crab's eyes are among the most studied in biology, and they work almost as well at night as by day.

senses.name: Compound eyes
senses.text: Each lateral eye is made of large units with individual photoreceptors big enough to record from. Linked photoreceptors dampen their neighbours' signals, sharpening edges before the image reaches the brain.

senses.name: Night vision
senses.text: A clock in the brain sends signals to the eyes at night that greatly raise their sensitivity, so horseshoe crabs can see at night nearly as well as by day.

senses.name: Extra eyes
senses.text: Besides the compound eyes, it has a pair of median eyes on top of the shell and three pairs of small 'rudimentary' eyes — larval eyes that persist into adulthood. Each type changes its light sensitivity over the day.

body.lede: Its body plan has barely changed in hundreds of millions of years, and some of its parts are unlike anything in a true crab.

systems.title: Copper-based blood
systems.text: Its blood carries oxygen with copper rather than iron. It is straw-coloured and turns blue when exposed to oxygen; its blood cells clot around bacterial toxins.

systems.title: Book gills
systems.text: Six page-like gills under the rear section each carry about 150 thin flaps, like the pages of a book. Beating them also lets the animal swim in an emergency.

systems.title: A tube-shaped heart
systems.text: The heart is a long tube running down the middle of the head shield and abdomen.

genome.lede: Sequencing shows that the horseshoe crab's ancestors copied their entire genome more than once — a rare event among invertebrates.

findings.title: Whole-genome duplications
findings.text: A 2025 chromosome-level assembly supports three whole-genome duplications unique to horseshoe crabs, none shared with spiders and scorpions.

findings.title: Doubled toxin detectors
findings.text: The genome carries tandem copies of Factors C and G, proteins in the pathway that detects bacterial toxins — the pathway behind the medical blood test.

findings.title: ZW sex chromosomes
findings.text: Females carry a ZW pair of sex chromosomes. The genome also records a steep population decline over the last 5 million years.

mind.lede: Horseshoe crabs have taught neuroscience more than their simple behaviour might suggest.

studies.title: One nerve fibre at a time
studies.text: Using the horseshoe crab's long, easily isolated optic nerve, H. Keffer Hartline and colleagues became the first to record nerve impulses from single optic nerve fibres.

studies.title: Lateral inhibition
studies.text: Hartline showed that excited photoreceptors suppress their neighbours, boosting contrast at edges. The discovery earned him a share of the 1967 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

studies.title: Courting a cement crab
studies.text: On a Massachusetts mating beach, males approached a cement model of a female from about 0.9 m away — about as well at night as in daylight. Females avoided it.

survival.lede: Adults are well armoured, but their eggs feed a whole coastline, and people take adults for bait and blood.

tactics.title: Righting itself
tactics.text: Flipped onto its back by the surf, a horseshoe crab uses its long tail to turn itself back over.

tactics.title: Spawning on the tides
tactics.text: Spawning usually coincides with high tides around full and new moons, when females come ashore to lay their eggs on the beach.

tactics.title: Many eggs
tactics.text: Females lay roughly 90,000 eggs a year in clusters, spread over repeated spawning visits.

threats.title: Bait harvest
threats.text: Horseshoe crabs are caught as bait for conch and eel fisheries; reported coastwide bait landings in 2024 were about 551,000 crabs.

threats.title: Biomedical bleeding
threats.text: In 2024 about 1.07 million crabs were collected for their blood, and an estimated 185,000 of them died as a result.

threats.title: Lost beaches
threats.text: Habitat loss and over-harvest leave the species vulnerable to local extinction, especially in New England and the Gulf of Maine.

life.lede: A horseshoe crab sheds its shell more than a dozen times and spends roughly a decade growing up before it spawns.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Females lay tiny green eggs in clusters of about 4,000 on spawning beaches. Some larvae overwinter in the nest and emerge the next spring.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: Hatchlings are about 3 mm across and have no tail. They swim in the plankton before settling on the bottom and starting to moult.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Young crabs stay on intertidal flats near their home beaches, then move into deeper water as they grow.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Males mature after about 16 moults at 8–9 years; females after 17 moults at 10–11 years. Adults live offshore and return to beaches to spawn.
